planning_labor_by_employment.csv:
MothersFathers

The buyer is employed. Among employed parents the gap is 1.75× (8.4 vs 4.8 min/day) — not the 3.0× that the all-parents figure reports, which is levered by non-employed mothers. BLS ATUS 2025, Tables 8A/8B, Tier A. BLS suspended collection 1 Oct – 12 Nov 2025; 2025 averages are 11-month and BLS states the effect “cannot be quantified.”
obligations_per_year.csv:
In the sourced-only floorBest estimate, conditional or estimated input

Emergency and urgent-care visits are unscheduled by definition and are excluded from any figure labelled “scheduled”. NCES publishes the school-meetings mean as a rounded integer (6), so decimals here are false precision — the band, not the point estimate, is the finding.
job_quadrants.csv:
Deep / episodic (Q1)Shallow / recurring (Q2–Q3)Weekly sports logistics — one row, 200 of 264

The deep-and-frequent quadrant (top right) is empty — depth and repetition are anti-correlated, so workflow ceremony can never be amortised. But the shallow total is dominated by a single row: weekly sports logistics is 200 of 264, and by the model’s own definition those are attendances, not captures. Excluding it, the honest comparison is ~23 obligations/yr vs ~16 deep objects — parity, not an order of magnitude.
seasonality_month_x_task.csv:
Flatness is not demand — the same task families on a shared volume scale

Summer camp’s worst month exceeds dental’s best by roughly 4.5×. A flat curve is steady, not large. Two caveats travel with this chart: fall registration’s volume is almost entirely a browse term (after school program), and school admin’s 30.7 is back to school, a retail term. Google Trends is not parent-scoped.
camp_forward_search.csv: Next-summer camp search roughly doubles in November, doubles again in December and triples into January — reproduced exactly across two independent cycles by a second verifier. The dead window is August–October: three months, not six. That hole is filled by two verticals already built and flagged off.
activity_supply_by_metro.csv:
Providers within 25 miLive sessions within 25 mi

Original measurement of ActivityHero’s public search index (2026-08-21, reproduced independently 2026-08-22). Nationally only 9,008 of 94,848 sessions (9.5%) are live. But provider rank and live rank disagree: LA has more providers than SF (5,686 vs 4,299) and a third the live sessions. An August pull is a seasonal trough — year-round classes survive it, summer-only supply does not — so this is a single-timepoint measurement, not a structural gradient. Vendor credential withheld per ActivityHero’s terms.

Both peak at 30–49 — the core parent cohort — and 18–29 is second-lowest on smart-speaker ownership. The intuition that younger parents are the voice audience is not supported. Pew Research Center, n=5,119 US adults, fielded 17–23 Feb 2026, Tier B.
email_options_scoring.csv: B′ and C both far outrank shipping Gmail OAuth alone. The ranking survived the correction; the original headline (69.5) did not — Google still requires the user to return and click Save Changes, and shows a week-long “someone else may have access to your account” banner precisely when B′’s pitch is trustworthiness.
channel_by_cohort.csv:
Gen Z parents (18-29)Millennial (30-45)Gen X (46-61)

Two facts do the work here. YouTube is the only near-parity channel (95/92/85), so it is the single-asset play. And Facebook inverts: it reaches Millennial and Gen X parents better than Gen Z ones, which is the opposite of the usual assumption about parent groups. Pew, n=5,119, fielded 17-23 Feb 2026, Tier B. Pew age bands are 18-29 / 30-49 / 50-64 and map only approximately to the cohort bands used elsewhere in this report.

Rank order follows the evidence, not judgement. Four of the top five are already built in whole or in part and are either buried, flag-gated, or scoped to one screen. That is the cheapest class of move available. The weakest-evidenced item, conversational voice, is the one the product currently ships most prominently.
